manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Constructing Linear Perspective in a Renaissance StudioI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Linear Perspective Construction of a City Street2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Renaissance Painting)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the method of linear perspective used in Renaissance painting by setting a single vanishing point on the horizon line and drawing orthogonal lines to construct the illusion of depth in a city street scene.II. Experimental EquipmentDrawing paper or panel, pencil and ruler, eraser, reference image of a city street (optional), studio lighting, camera mounted on a tripod with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the drawing surface on an easel or table in a studio setting. Fix the camera on a tripod facing the drawing surface and lock the focus and framing.2. Establish Horizon: Draw a straight horizontal line across the paper at eye level to represent the horizon.3. Set Vanishing Point: Mark a single point at the center of the horizon line; this will serve as the vanishing point.4. Draw Orthogonals: From the vanishing point, use a ruler to draw multiple straight lines radiating downward toward the foreground, defining the edges of the street and buildings.5. Construct Forms: Add vertical and horizontal lines between orthogonals to suggest buildings, windows, and street elements.6. Recording: Allow the camera to capture the drawing process in time-lapse, without changing focus or position.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Blank paper with only the horizon line and a single marked point.2. During Drawing: As orthogonals are added, the flat surface begins to suggest depth, with lines visually converging toward the vanishing point.3. Final State: The completed sketch clearly resembles a city street receding into space, creating a convincing illusion of depth.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesLinear perspective is based on geometric optics and human visual perception. Parallel lines in the real world appear to converge at a single vanishing point on the horizon when represented on a flat surface. By fixing the viewer’s eye level (horizon) and consistently aligning orthogonals to one vanishing point, Renaissance artists created realistic spatial depth in two-dimensional paintings.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Renaissance linear perspective with a single vanishing point. Minimum assumptions: a fixed viewer eye level (horizon), one vanishing point, and straight orthogonal lines governed by simple geometry. Expected phenomena storyline: (1) horizon and vanishing point established; (2) orthogonals drawn from foreground toward the vanishing point; (3) forms constructed between orthogonals; (4) depth illusion emerges. Visibility constraints: camera remains fixed and focused so convergence and spatial consistency can be visually verified in the time-lapse.
